name: 74HC245 Octal Bus Transceiver
summary: Eight bidirectional buffers with a direction pin and a tri-state enable. What you put between a CPU bus and anything you do not fully trust.
notes: DIR picks which way the data flows: high sends A to B, low sends B to A. It is not an enable, and getting it backwards means two drivers fighting.
OE is active low and tri-states all eight lines when high. Wire it from your address decode so the transceiver only drives during its own bus cycle.
The A and B pins are mirrored across the package: A1 to A8 run down pins 2 to 9, B8 to B1 run down pins 11 to 18. B1 sits opposite A8, not A1. Wire from the numbers.
Each output drives about 6 mA, far more than a microcontroller pin, which is the point when a bus has to reach across a backplane or a ribbon cable.
It does not level shift on its own: A and B share one supply. For a genuine level translation use a 74LVC245 powered at the lower rail, which is 5 V tolerant on its inputs.
Commonly used simply as a strong output buffer with DIR tied high and OE grounded.

pins.name: DIR
pins.note: High: A drives B. Low: B drives A.

pins.name: B8
pins.note: B8 sits opposite A1, not A8. The two buses run in opposite directions across the package.

pins.name: OE
pins.note: Ground to drive. High tri-states all eight lines.

pins.name: VCC
pins.note: 100 nF at the pin. Eight lines switching at once is a real current spike.

circuit.title: Minimum circuit

parts.why: Output enable is active low. Left floating the buffer stays in high impedance and looks like a dead chip.
Direction high sends A to B. Drive this pin instead if the bus has to turn around.
Supply decoupling at the pin, and it matters here: eight outputs can switch at once.

circuit.note: Both sides are driven outputs when enabled, so never tie DIR by accident on a shared bus: two buffers pointing at each other is a short between whatever is driving them.
